subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 4, the last unit of Year 5. In this unit you will look at how a whole computer system works, from the moment it takes something in to the moment it does something useful. You already use computer systems every single day — a phone, a tablet, a laptop, a television, even the little computer inside a microwave or a car. By the end of this unit you will understand what is really happening inside all of them.

A computer system does three big jobs: it takes in input, it does some processing (thinking), and it gives out an output (an action or some information). To do all of this it needs devices to collect input and devices to produce output, and it needs somewhere to store data. In the newest and cleverest systems, a special kind of software called artificial intelligence helps the computer make choices that seem almost human.

There are four parts to this unit, and it is best to work through them in order because each one builds on the last. First you will explore input and output devices (4.1) — the parts that let a computer sense the world and act on it. Then you will discover how data is stored (4.2) as tiny 1s and 0s, and how we measure it. Next you will learn how a computer processes data (4.3) using the input-process-output model. Finally you will investigate artificial intelligence (4.4) and think carefully about how to use it responsibly and fairly.

concepts.title: Input and Output Devices
concepts.explanation:
Almost every computer needs input. Input is how a computer knows what is happening around it, so that it can make choices or carry out actions. This is very much like the way you use your eyes and ears to see and hear what is happening in the world. A device that provides input to a computer is called an input device.

You already know several input devices. A touchscreen is an input device — you find them on smartphones and tablets. A mouse is an input device: when you move the mouse, the movement is the input, and the cursor moves around the screen. A keyboard is an input device too: it lets you enter text, numbers and symbols to tell the computer what you want it to do. A microphone is an input device that takes in sound.

Sensors: giving a computer its senses

A sensor is a special and very important type of input device. Sensors sense and measure changes in the world around them. If input devices are how a computer notices things, then sensors are the computer's senses. Here are two everyday examples:

An oven uses a temperature sensor to sense how hot it is inside. When the oven reaches the correct temperature, the heater is switched off.

Many cars have a light sensor. When it senses that it is getting dark outside, the car's headlights come on automatically. When it is light again, they switch off.

For the smart garden, the team will use three sensors: a moisture sensor to sense how wet the soil is, a temperature sensor to sense how hot the air is, and a light sensor to sense how bright it is. Together, these sensors let the garden 'feel' its surroundings, just as you feel the sun and the rain.
concepts.example: Input devices can be connected directly to a computer, sitting right next to it like a mouse or keyboard. But input devices can also be connected remotely. Remote means far away. A remote input device connects to a computer over the internet, so it does not have to be anywhere near the computer at all — it could be in another city or even another country.

concepts.title: Remote input devices are useful in four main situations:
concepts.explanation:
When we want to collect data over a long time — days, months or even years.

When we want to collect input from a place that is a long way from our computer.

When it is not safe for a human to use a device by hand.

When collecting the data automatically makes life easier or more efficient.

Think of a scientist studying how the climate is changing. They need to measure the temperature in many places around the world, every hour of every day, and compare them. One person could never do this alone. Instead they place a temperature sensor in each place and connect to them all remotely over the internet. In the same way, a power station uses sensors to measure temperature and how much electricity is being made, all the time and in many places at once.

Remote input devices are also perfect for dangerous places. Scientists cannot get close to a volcano when it erupts, because of the hot lava and poisonous gas, so they use remote sensors and stay safely far away. Space scientists use remote sensors carried on telescopes, space stations, and robots like the Mars Rover, to collect data from millions of kilometres away and send it back to Earth. And rescue robots with cameras and sensors can search a collapsed building, so that people do not have to enter a dangerous place themselves.
concepts.example: You may even have remote input devices at home. A smart plug can switch itself on and off, and smart lights can change when you tell them to. These 'smart' devices use sensors so that we can control them, sometimes from the other side of the room and sometimes from the other side of the city.

concepts.title: Using more than one sensor to stay safe
concepts.explanation:
Sometimes, using only one sensor is a risk — especially when the data is important for keeping people safe. What if the sensor breaks, or sends the wrong reading? Imagine you check one temperature sensor to decide whether to bring your coat to school. If it tells you the wrong temperature, you might leave your coat at home and then shiver all day.

To solve this problem, important systems use two or more sensors to measure the same thing. Suppose we use three temperature sensors. If one says it is hot but the other two say it is cold, the computer can work out that one sensor is probably broken, and that it is most likely cold outside because two sensors agree. The computer ignores the odd reading and trusts the others. Many important control systems work exactly this way, comparing several sensors so that a single mistake cannot cause a disaster.

Once a computer has taken in input and processed it, it produces an output. Output is any information or action based on the input. An output device is the hardware that produces that output. A screen shows pictures and words; a speaker makes sound; a printer prints onto paper; a lamp gives light; a buzzer makes a warning noise.

Input and output work together. When you move the mouse (input), the cursor moves on the screen (output). When you touch a touchscreen (input), the screen shows where you touched (output). When a motion sensor on an automatic door detects someone (input), a motor turns and the door opens (output). Here are some everyday outputs in the world around you:
concepts.example: A robot changing the way it moves.

concepts.title: Actuators
concepts.explanation:
An actuator is a special type of output device. While a screen or a speaker gives out information, an actuator gives out movement. Actuators are parts of a machine that open, close or move physical objects. A simple rule helps you spot them: if a device makes something move, it is probably an actuator.

You have seen actuators without realising it. At a supermarket checkout, the moving belt that carries the shopping towards the till is an actuator — it is a motor joined to a rubber belt. On an aeroplane, an actuator moves the flaps on the wings. In a hydroelectric dam, sensors detect how much electricity is needed, a computer works out how much water to let through, and an actuator opens the water gates. For the smart garden, the water pump is an actuator: when the computer decides the soil is too dry, the actuator switches the water on.
concepts.example: Actuators can also make life easier for people. A voice-controlled door opener can help someone who finds it hard to move: they simply ask, and an actuator opens the door for them.

concepts.title: Input devices and output devices side by side
concepts.explanation:
It is easy to muddle up input and output, so keep this comparison in your mind. The big idea is the direction: input goes INTO the computer, output comes OUT of it.

It can take up to about 22 minutes for a radio signal to travel from Earth all the way to the Mars Rover. That means when scientists send the rover an instruction, they must wait — the rover cannot be steered second by second like a toy car. It has to be clever enough to do a lot on its own.

What they do — Send data INTO the computer · Send information or actions OUT of the computer

Direction — Into the computer (the computer notices something) · Out of the computer (the computer does something)

When they are used — First — the computer needs input to know what is happening · Last — after the computer has processed the input

concepts.title: How Is Data Stored?
concepts.explanation:
A storage device lets a computer save data permanently. 'Permanently' means the data stays even when you switch the computer off, until you choose to delete it. This is how your photos, your schoolwork and your favourite songs are still there when you turn your device back on. There are many different types of storage device, and the smart garden will need one to keep all its daily readings.

Some storage devices live inside a computer or other device — these are called internal storage devices. The storage inside a tablet, a smartphone or a desktop computer is internal. Other storage devices are external, meaning they live outside the main case in their own case. An external hard drive and a memory stick are examples of external storage.
concepts.example: External storage devices have a hard outer case to protect the data inside, so that a memory stick is not damaged if you drop it. They are very useful for two reasons: they add extra space, and they let you move files from one computer to another. Laptops are made to be small and light, so there is not much room inside for storage — which is why people so often add external storage to a laptop.

concepts.title: The three types of storage device
concepts.explanation:
There are three different ways to store data, so there are three types of storage device: magnetic, optical and solid state. They each store the data differently, and each has good points and bad points.

A magnetic storage device uses magnets and thin metal discs. The discs are stacked on top of each other a bit like a pile of pancakes, and a magnet writes the data onto them. Magnetic storage is common and usually cheap, and it is often used in servers (the powerful computers that store websites). Its weakness is that it has moving parts, which can be damaged if it is dropped. The most common magnetic device is the hard disk drive (HDD), which can be internal or external and can store hundreds of films.

An optical storage device uses circular plastic discs — CDs and DVDs. A laser (a thin beam of very powerful light) burns tiny marks onto the plastic disc, and the same laser can read those marks back and turn them into numbers the computer understands. Optical discs are easy to scratch and damage, and they are rarely used now, because most people stream or download music and films instead. You might not have a single DVD at home.

A solid state storage device uses electronic circuits to store data. It was invented more recently, and it is the most expensive type. Its great advantage is that it has no moving parts, so it is much less likely to be damaged if it is dropped, and it works much faster than magnetic or optical storage. Solid state storage is used in most modern laptops, tablets and phones. A memory stick is a small, portable solid state device — very handy, but so small it is easy to lose.

How is data actually stored? Binary!

We now know storage devices save data. But how is the data itself stored? The answer is binary. Binary is a number system that uses only two digits: 1 and 0. Everything a computer stores — every letter, photo, song and video — is really just a huge string of 1s and 0s.
concepts.example: Why only two digits? Because a computer's memory is made of millions of tiny switches, and a switch can only be in one of two states: on or off. We write an on switch as 1 and an off switch as 0. Picture a row of light switches on a wall:

concepts.title: On/off switches become the binary digits 1 and 0
concepts.explanation:
The binary value stored in one switch — a single 1 or 0 — is called a bit. A bit is the smallest unit of data storage there is. Each type of storage device has its own clever way of remembering whether a bit is a 1 or a 0. In optical storage, for example, a mark on the disc means 1 and no mark means 0.

When you save a file, the computer converts it into binary. A text document, a photo, a spreadsheet — all of them are stored as long lines of 1s and 0s. Here is what eight bits of storage might look like on an optical disc, where six spots have no mark and two spots have a mark:

Eight bits stored as marks: this reads 00000011

No mark No mark No mark No mark No mark No mark Mark Mark

That group of eight bits is so useful that it has its own name: a byte. A byte is exactly 8 bits. One byte is enough to store a single letter, like the letter 'A'. From the byte, all the bigger storage units are built.

Because everything is made of bits, we need units to measure how much data there is — just as we use grams and kilograms to measure weight. Here are the units you need for Year 5, from the smallest to the largest. Notice that each big unit is 1,000 times the one before it.

There are two simple rules hidden in that table. To go from bytes to bits, multiply by 8 (because 1 byte = 8 bits). To climb one step up the ladder — bytes to KB, KB to MB, MB to GB — multiply by 1,000. To go back down the ladder, divide by 1,000. If you learn the order bit, byte, KB, MB, GB by heart, every storage question becomes easy. (When you reach Year 6 you will add one more step: the terabyte, which is 1,000 GB.)

When we convert, we change one unit into another. Follow the rules and it is just multiplying or dividing. For example, how many kilobytes are there in 10 MB?

So 10 MB is 10 x 1,000 KB, which is 10,000 KB.

Try the same idea the other way. How many bytes are in 3 KB? Since 1 KB is 1,000 bytes, 3 KB is 3,000 bytes. And how many bits are in 1 byte? Always 8. The Practice document has many more of these to try, so do not worry if it feels new — you will soon be quick at it.

Data travelling through the internet can move at around 200,000 kilometres every second. The Earth is about 40,000 kilometres around, so in a single second that data could travel all the way around the whole planet roughly five times. This is why a sensor on Uncle Tariq's farm can send a reading to a computer almost instantly.

Data stays on a storage device until you delete it. So if you throw away an old phone or memory stick without clearing it, someone could still read your private data. Always delete your files and personal information from old storage devices before you give them away. Protecting your own and other people's information is a kind and responsible thing to do.

concepts.title: Processing Data
concepts.explanation:
Every computer system does three things in order: it takes in input, it does some processing, and it gives out an output. We call this the input-process-output model, and it is one of the most important ideas in computing. Let us look at each stage.

Input comes from an input device — perhaps a button, or a sensor. It tells the computer what is happening. Some sensors send data all the time, while others only send data when something happens, like a button being pressed. Processing is when the computer decides what to do about the input. A program inside the computer makes the decision, and the way it decides depends on how it was programmed. Finally, the computer produces an output — perhaps it flashes a light, sounds a buzzer, or turns an actuator on or off.

A worked example: the office fan

Imagine an office with an automatic fan. A temperature sensor sends the computer data about how hot the room is — that is the input. The computer's program processes this data and works out that the office is too hot. So the computer sends an instruction to switch the fan on — that is the output. When the room cools down, the same three stages happen again and the fan switches off. (Computers measure temperature using sensors called thermistors, which change the flow of electricity depending on how hot they are.)

Humans use input-process-output too

You use this model yourself, all day long, without ever thinking about it. You have five senses that collect input: sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch. Your brain processes what your senses tell you, and then your body produces an output. Here is one example using your hearing:

Input — you hear a fire alarm ringing.

Process — your brain understands there may be a fire, and sends signals telling your body to move.

Output — you get up and walk to the fire exit.

Seeing the model in your own body makes it much easier to spot in machines. A computer's sensor is like your ears, its program is like your brain, and its actuator is like your legs.

Processing means making choices

When a computer processes data, it is really making choices. We program those choices by writing an IF statement — exactly like the ones you wrote earlier in Year 5. An IF statement lets a computer choose between different actions. Look at this short algorithm for the smart garden's window:

A simple IF...THEN...ELSE choice

Can you find the three stages? The input is the temperature reading. The process is the computer checking 'is it warm?' and choosing. The output is the window opening or closing. Real programs usually have many more choices than this, which lets a computer handle far more complicated situations.

Input-process-output all around us

Once you know the model, you will start to see it everywhere. Study this table carefully — every row is a real computer system split into its three stages.

A single button on a games controller is an input device that only sends data when it is pressed. A temperature sensor is different — it can send data all the time, even when nothing is changing. Both are inputs, but they behave in very different ways.

concepts.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI)
concepts.explanation:
Can computers be as clever as humans?

As humans, we do many things automatically, without stopping to think. If we see someone in trouble, we often try to help straight away. We are also very good at learning: if you eat an ice cream too fast and it gives you a headache, you learn to eat the next one more slowly. This is intelligence — using our knowledge and skills in a sensible way, and changing what we do based on what we learn.

Ordinary computers are not like this. They run programs written by humans, and those programs usually do not change. The computer can only carry out the exact commands it was given. That means an ordinary computer, on its own, is not intelligent — it just follows instructions very quickly and very accurately.

What is artificial intelligence?

Computer scientists have found ways to write programs that let computers think and act more like humans. This is called artificial intelligence, or AI for short. Artificial intelligence is a way to simulate human intelligence — 'simulate' means to copy or recreate something.
concepts.example: A computer with AI can do two special things. First, it can carry out tasks on its own, making choices as it goes. Second — and this is the amazing part — it can learn. It can change how it responds to different inputs, so that it gets better and better over time. This learning is called machine learning. The more the AI is used, the more it learns, and the more helpful it becomes.

concepts.explanation:

To truly copy human intelligence, we would need to add many, many more lines of code so the robot could handle chair legs, stairs, socks on the floor, and everything else in a real room. Real AI programs can be enormous.

concepts.title: Robots and AI are not the same thing
concepts.explanation:
It is easy to think that 'robots' and 'AI' mean the same thing, but they are different areas of computing. Most robots follow fixed algorithms that never change — they do the same job the same way every time. AI is about changing how a computer responds to its inputs. Sometimes AI is added to a robot to help it adapt to its surroundings, but plenty of robots have no AI at all, and plenty of AI runs on ordinary computers with no robot in sight.

Making good choices: predicting and being fair

Every programmer working on AI has to think about two big things. The first is helping the program learn, predict, and make better choices in the future. A large part of AI is predicting what will happen next and choosing the best action for the input it receives — and then learning from whether that choice worked.

The second thing is making sure the program's decisions are fair and suitable. Sometimes, by accident, programmers create an AI that is biased. Being biased means treating some people or choices unfairly. Imagine you fill in a form to join a basketball club, and the form is checked by a biased AI. The AI has learnt that very tall people are usually good at basketball, so it decides you cannot join because you are not tall enough. That is unfair, because it is judging you only on your height and not on how well you actually play. Programmers must work hard to find and remove bias like this.

Artificial intelligence is used all around us, often without us noticing. Here are some examples you may already have met:

Music and video suggestions. When you listen to songs online, AI learns what you like and suggests more songs you might enjoy.

Helping people with disabilities. AI can respond to a person's voice to open doors, switch on lights, or read text aloud. Someone who finds it hard to see can speak to their phone, and the AI understands, opens a map, and gives spoken directions.

Smart homes. AI can learn the time you usually wake up and have the lights on ready, or learn the temperature you like and warm the room for you.
concepts.example: This is where the team can help Uncle Tariq. Across East Africa, some farmers now use apps powered by AI that study years of weather and soil data to predict the best time to plant and water their crops. Such an app could help Tariq use his water carefully and get a better harvest. But the team will be honest with him too: an AI can only be as good as the data it learns from, it can make mistakes, and it should support a farmer's own knowledge of his land, not replace it.

concepts.title: Predictive text and speech to text
concepts.explanation:
Two kinds of AI live inside most phones. The first is predictive text. As you type a message, it reads what you have written and suggests the next word. It works by using probability — how likely something is to happen. If you usually write 'Hello! How are you?', the phone learns this and offers 'How' and 'are' and 'you' before you even type them, with your most common choices appearing first.

The second is speech to text. Here the computer learns how your voice sounds and which words you use often, and turns your speech into written text in a message or document. Sometimes it gets a word wrong or puts a full stop in the wrong place. When you correct it, the AI learns from the correction and is less likely to make the same mistake again — machine learning in action. Speech to text is a huge help to people who find a keyboard difficult to use.

Talking like humans: the Turing test

A big challenge of AI is getting a computer to talk like a human. Back in 1950, a British mathematician and computer scientist called Alan Turing described a famous test for this. In the Turing test, a person has a conversation without being able to see who they are talking to. If they cannot tell whether they are talking to a human or a computer, the computer is said to have passed the test.

Today, many websites let you 'chat' to a computer to get help. These are called virtual assistants: you type a question and the computer types back a reply. Your own AI tutor for this course is a modern, very advanced example of a computer that can talk with you and help you learn.

AI is powerful and useful, but it is not perfect and it is not magic. Because humans write and train it, an AI can contain mistakes, it can be biased, and it can sound very sure of itself while being completely wrong. So we must use it wisely and responsibly. Here is a fair and balanced way to think about it:

Always check important answers. Would you trust an AI to pick your songs? Probably yes. Would you trust it, with no human checking, to perform an operation in a hospital? That needs great care. The more serious the task, the more a human must stay in charge.

Be honest. If AI helps you with schoolwork, say so, and make sure you still understand the work yourself. Passing off an AI's writing as your own is not honest.

Be fair and kind. Think about whether an AI is treating everyone fairly, and speak up if it is not.

Protect privacy. Do not share other people's private information with an AI.
concepts.example: Thinking carefully about right and wrong, being honest, and being fair to others are important values in every community and in our daily lives. They matter just as much when we usethe newest technology as they do everywhere else.

activities.title: Classify the devices in a system
activities.materials: A computer or tablet with Scratch, plus paper and a pencil for planning
steps: It could be the smart garden, an automatic door at a shop, a fridge with a temperature alarm, or a farm watering system. Choose a real system to study.
List its input devices and its output devices in two columns, and mark any actuator.
Split it into input-process-output, writing one clear sentence for each stage.
Expected Result (Task 1)

A correct two-column list of inputs and outputs, the actuator clearly marked, and a sensible input-process-output breakdown. For a fridge alarm: input = temperature sensor; process = the computer checks if it is too warm; output = a buzzer sounds.

activities.title: Estimate the storage it needs
activities.materials: A computer or tablet with Scratch, plus paper and a pencil for planning
steps: Imagine your system saves one reading every hour, all day and all night.
If each reading takes about 1 KB, work out roughly how much storage it uses in one day (24 readings), and in one week.
Write your answer in the sensible unit (bytes, KB or MB), and say whether an internal or external storage device would suit it.
Expected Result (Task 2)

24 readings a day at 1 KB each is about 24 KB a day, and about 168 KB in a week — small enough for ordinary internal storage. The best answers show the multiplication and choose a sensible unit and storage type.

esafety.title: Keep personal information private
esafety.text: Your full name, address, school, phone number, birthday and passwords are personal information. Never type them into a game, an app or a website, and never send them to someone you only know online.

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

rules.title: Remember
rules.text: Top Facts to Keep in Your Head Input goes INTO the computer; output comes OUT. A sensor is an input; an actuator is an output that moves things. A touchscreen is both an input and an output device. Three storage types: magnetic (cheap, moving parts), optical (laser and disc), solid state (fast, most expensive, no moving parts). Storage ladder: bit, byte, KB, MB, GB (and TB in Year 6). Up = multiply by 1,000, down = divide by 1,000, and 1 byte = 8 bits. Computers store everything as binary — just 1s and 0s — because their memory is made of on/off switches.

commonMistakes: a screen is an input device. Truth: a plain screen is an output device (it shows things). A touchscreen is special because it is BOTH an input and an output device.

bit, byte, KB, MB, GB. Say it out loud until it is automatic, and remember multiply by 1,000 to go up, divide by 1,000 to go down, and 1 byte = 8 bits.
